rationale.intervention_reconstruction: The hypothesis proposes microalloying with Y and Hf, while the paper alloyed with Zr. These are different reactive elements, so it is a different specific lever within the same kind of intervention (alloying addition).
rationale.condition_agreement: The hypothesis mentions conventional casting, extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive environments (molten salt). The paper used as-cast alloys, room-temperature compression, nanoindentation creep, and electrochemical corrosion in 3.5 wt% NaCl. The testing regimes differ significantly (molten salt vs. NaCl, thermal cycling vs. room temperature).
rationale.mechanism_agreement: The hypothesis invokes reactive-element effects on oxide scale adhesion and grain-boundary stabilization. The paper's mechanism involves solid-solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening via Ni7Zr2, and a Zr-rich passive layer. These are different general classes of mechanism (oxide scale adhesion vs. precipitation/dispersion strengthening and passive film formation).
rationale.outcome_agreement: The hypothesis predicts enhanced thermal stability, lower room-temperature creep, and improved corrosion resistance while retaining strength-ductility balance. The paper found an optimum in strength and creep resistance at moderate Zr, with a trade-off in corrosion resistance, and did not test thermal cycling. The predicted outcome is only vaguely aligned in general terms (improved corrosion and creep) but differs in specifics and trade-offs.
